CheckTitle: AI Search service has public network access disabled
Description: **Azure AI Search service** limits its data-plane endpoint by disabling **public network access**. This evaluation checks whether the service only permits connections via **private endpoints** or narrowly scoped, explicitly allowed sources.
Risk:
Internet-reachable search endpoints impact CIA:
- Confidentiality: unauthorized queries reveal indexed data/metadata
- Integrity: stolen admin/query keys allow index changes or deletions
- Availability: abuse and scanning drive throttling and outages

Code.Terraform:
```hcl
# Disable public network access for Azure AI Search
resource "azurerm_search_service" "<example_resource_name>" {
  name                = "<example_resource_name>"
  resource_group_name = "<example_resource_name>"
  location            = "<location>"
  sku                 = "basic"

  public_network_access_enabled = false  # CRITICAL: Disables public access to pass the check
}
```
Code.CLI: az search service update --name <service_name> --resource-group <resource_group_name> --public-access disabled
Code.Other:
1. In the Azure portal, open your AI Search service
2. Go to Settings > Networking
3. Under Public network access, select Disabled
4. Click Save
5. Wait a few minutes and re-run the check

Recommendation.Text: Set `Public network access: Disabled`. Prefer **Private Link** and restrict any residual exposure to specific sources only. Use **least privilege** with Microsoft Entra ID RBAC instead of keys. Apply **defense in depth** with IP rules/trusted services, enable logs, and review access lists regularly.

CheckTitle: AKS cluster has RBAC enabled
Description:
**AKS clusters** with **Kubernetes RBAC** enforce authorization through roles and bindings mapped to identities and groups.

This evaluates whether the cluster has RBAC enabled to control access to namespaces and cluster-wide resources.
Risk: Without **Kubernetes RBAC**, authorization becomes overly broad, weakening **least privilege**. Compromised credentials could read secrets, alter workloads, or delete services, impacting **confidentiality**, **integrity**, and **availability**, and enabling lateral movement across the cluster.

Code.Other:
1. In Azure portal, go to Kubernetes services > Create (or edit your deployment template)
2. On the Authentication tab, set Kubernetes RBAC to Enabled
3. Review + Create to deploy (re-create the cluster if the setting can't be changed on an existing one)

Recommendation.Text:
Enable **Kubernetes RBAC** and design permissions with **least privilege**: scope roles to namespaces, grant access via groups, apply deny-by-default, and separate duties for admins and operators.

Integrate with **Microsoft Entra ID** and review/audit role bindings to maintain **defense in depth**.

CheckTitle: AKS cluster nodes do not have public IP addresses
Description: **AKS agent pools** use only private addressing, with node public IP assignment disabled (`enableNodePublicIP=false`). Clusters where any pool assigns a public IP to nodes are identified.
Risk: **Public node IPs** expose worker VMs to Internet scanning and exploit attempts against OS or kubelet services. Successful compromise can lead to stolen secrets and images (**confidentiality**), workload tampering (**integrity**), and node/resource exhaustion via DDoS or cryptomining (**availability**).

Code.Other:
1. In the Azure portal, go to Kubernetes services > <your AKS cluster> > Node pools
2. For any node pool showing Node public IP: Enabled, click Add node pool
3. Create the new pool with the same size/count; set Node public IP to Disabled (or uncheck Enable node public IP)
4. Wait until the new pool is Ready
5. If replacing a system pool, set the new pool to Mode: System (or Set as default system pool)
6. Delete the old node pool(s) that had Node public IP enabled
7. Verify all node pools show Node public IP: Disabled

Recommendation.Text: Disable **public node IPs** on all agent pools (`enableNodePublicIP=false`) and route egress via a **NAT gateway** or **Azure Firewall**. Apply **least privilege** with NSGs blocking Internet ingress, use **private endpoints** and **bastion/VPN** for admin access, and adopt **defense in depth** with continuous hardening and monitoring.

CheckTitle: AKS cluster has a private endpoint and node public access is disabled
Description:
**AKS clusters** expose a **private control plane FQDN** and agent pools have `enable_node_public_ip=false`.

The evaluation focuses on the presence of a private FQDN and the absence of public IPs on nodes.
Risk:
Exposed node IPs or a publicly reachable API increase attack surface, impacting **confidentiality** and **integrity**.
- Internet scans reach kubelet, NodePort, or management agents
- Exploits enable RCE and **lateral movement**
- Metadata/secret theft leads to **credential compromise**

**Availability** is at risk from DDoS on exposed endpoints.

Code.Other:
1. In the Azure portal, go to Azure Kubernetes Service and select your cluster
2. Go to Networking > API server access
3. Set Private cluster to Enabled and click Save
4. Go to Node pools, open each pool, select Networking, set Public IP per node to Disabled, and Save
5. Repeat step 4 for all node pools

Recommendation.Text:
Adopt **private clusters** and eliminate node public IPs:
- Set `enable_node_public_ip=false` on all pools
- Use **Private Link** or peered VNets with VPN/ExpressRoute for admin access
- If public API is unavoidable, restrict with IP ranges and strong auth
- Enforce NSGs/firewalls and **least privilege** for layered defense

CheckTitle: AKS cluster has network policy enabled
Description: **AKS clusters** enforce **Kubernetes network policies** so that pod-to-pod traffic is governed by explicit ingress and egress rules. The finding evaluates whether a cluster has network policy enforcement enabled to support fine-grained, label-based segmentation between workloads.
Risk:
Without network policy, pods can talk to any pod:
- Easy lateral movement after a pod compromise
- Unrestricted access to backend services and data
- Covert exfiltration/C2 via East-West traffic

This harms **confidentiality** and **integrity** and amplifies the blast radius of runtime exploits.

Code.CLI: az aks update --resource-group <RESOURCE_GROUP> --name <CLUSTER_NAME> --network-policy calico
Code.Other:
1. In Azure Portal, go to Kubernetes services and select your cluster
2. Open Networking (or Settings > Networking)
3. Set Network policy to Azure or Calico
4. Click Save to apply

Recommendation.Text:
Enable **network policy enforcement** and apply **least privilege** segmentation.
- Start with a `deny-all` baseline, allow only required flows
- Define both ingress and egress policies
- Use consistent labels/namespaces
- Layer with **defense in depth** (RBAC, node isolation, private networking) for zero-trust East-West control.

Notes: Network Policy requires the Network Policy add-on. This add-on is included automatically when a cluster with Network Policy is created, but for an existing cluster, needs to be added prior to enabling Network Policy. Enabling/Disabling Network Policy causes a rolling update of all cluster nodes, similar to performing a cluster upgrade. This operation is long-running and will block other operations on the cluster (including delete) until it has run to completion. If Network Policy is used, a cluster must have at least 2 nodes of type n1-standard-1 or higher. The recommended minimum size cluster to run Network Policy enforcement is 3 n1-standard-1 instances. Enabling Network Policy enforcement consumes additional resources in nodes. Specifically, it increases the memory footprint of the kube-system process by approximately 128MB, and requires approximately 300 millicores of CPU.

CheckTitle: No potential LLM Jacking attacks detected across all Azure API Management instances
Description: **API Management** diagnostic logs in Log Analytics are analyzed for **LLM-related operations**. Requests are grouped by caller IP, the number of distinct monitored actions (e.g., `ChatCompletions_Create`, `ImageGenerations_Create`) within a configurable `minutes` window is measured, and that ratio is compared to a `threshold` to surface anomalous multi-action patterns.
Risk:
Concentrated LLM activity from one IP indicates **automation or leaked credentials**.
- **Availability/cost**: rapid token burn and quota exhaustion
- **Confidentiality**: exposure of prompts/completions and model details
- **Integrity**: abuse of deployment/model actions enabling unauthorized changes or mass content generation

Code.Terraform:
```hcl
# Global APIM policy that blocks a specific IP
resource "azurerm_api_management_policy" "<example_resource_name>" {
  api_management_id = "<example_resource_id>"

  # Critical: Policy XML that blocks the offending IP by returning 403
  xml_content = <<XML
<policies>
  <inbound>
    <base />
    <choose>
      <!-- Critical: Block offending IP to stop LLM jacking -->
      <when condition="@(context.Request.IpAddress == \"<OFFENDING_IP>\")">
        <return-response>
          <set-status code="403" reason="Forbidden" />
        </return-response>
      </when>
    </choose>
  </inbound>
  <backend><base /></backend>
  <outbound><base /></outbound>
  <on-error><base /></on-error>
</policies>
XML
}
```
Code.Other:
1. In the Azure portal, open your API Management instance
2. Go to APIs > All APIs
3. Click Policies (Inbound processing)
4. Add a when block to block the offending IP:
   - Condition: @(context.Request.IpAddress == "<OFFENDING_IP>")
   - Action: return-response with status 403 Forbidden
5. Save the policy
6. Re-run the scan after the detection window elapses to confirm PASS

Recommendation.Text:
Adopt **defense in depth** for LLM APIs:
- Enforce **least privilege**; isolate management from inference
- Prefer **managed identities** over keys; rotate secrets
- Apply **quotas**, rate limiting, and IP allowlisting; use private access
- Alert on anomalous action diversity; review logs

*Tune `threshold` and `minutes` for your environment.*

Notes: This check requires: 1. APIM diagnostic logging to be enabled and configured to send logs to Log Analytics workspace 2. Log Analytics workspace ID and key to be configured in the audit configuration 3. Appropriate permissions to query Log Analytics workspace

CheckTitle: Web app requires incoming client certificates
Description: **Azure App Service apps** enforce **mutual TLS** when `client certificate mode` is set to `Required`, meaning every inbound request must present a valid client certificate that the app can validate.
Risk: Without **mTLS**, clients aren't cryptographically authenticated at the transport layer. Adversaries can reach endpoints using spoofed sources or stolen tokens, leading to unauthorized data access (confidentiality), request tampering (integrity), and automated abuse that degrades service (availability).

Code.Terraform:
```hcl
# Require client certificates for the App Service (use azurerm_linux_web_app or azurerm_windows_web_app)
resource "azurerm_linux_web_app" "<example_resource_name>" {
  name                = "<example_resource_name>"
  location            = "<example_location>"
  resource_group_name = "<example_resource_name>"
  service_plan_id     = "<example_resource_id>"

  client_certificate_enabled = true      # Critical: enables mutual TLS
  client_certificate_mode    = "Required" # Critical: enforces client certs (passes the check)

  site_config {}
}
```
Code.CLI: az webapp update --resource-group <RESOURCE_GROUP_NAME> --name <APP_NAME> --set clientCertEnabled=true clientCertMode=Required
Code.Other:
1. Open Azure Portal and go to App Services
2. Select your web app
3. Go to Configuration > General settings
4. Under Client certificate mode, select Required
5. Click Save

Recommendation.Text:
Set `client certificate mode` to `Required` and validate client certs in application logic (issuer, validity, revocation).

Enforce HTTPS only, avoid broad exclusion paths, and manage certs via a trusted CA with rotation and revocation. Apply **least privilege** and **zero trust**, layering with private access or IP restrictions *as needed*.

Notes: Utilizing and maintaining client certificates will require additional work to obtain and manage replacement and key rotation.

CheckTitle: App Service app has App Service Authentication enabled
Description:
**Azure App Service** can enforce built-in **Authentication/Authorization** (Easy Auth) so requests are authenticated by a provider before reaching app code.

This evaluates whether platform auth is enabled for the app and an identity provider is configured.
Risk: Without platform **authentication**, apps may accept **anonymous requests**, enabling unauthorized access to APIs and data. Attackers can enumerate endpoints and bypass weak app checks, risking data exposure (C), unauthorized changes (I), and automated abuse impacting availability (A).

Code.CLI: az webapp auth update --resource-group <RESOURCE_GROUP_NAME> --name <APP_NAME> --enabled true
Code.Other:
1. Sign in to the Azure Portal and go to App Services
2. Select <APP_NAME> and open Authentication
3. Click Add identity provider, choose Microsoft, and click Add
4. Save changes

This enables App Service Authentication for the app

Recommendation.Text: Enable App Service **Authentication/Authorization** and set `Require authentication` for unauthenticated requests. Use **Microsoft Entra** or a trusted IdP, restrict tenants/audiences, enforce HTTPS, and apply **least privilege** with role/claim checks and Conditional Access for defense-in-depth. Avoid `Allow anonymous requests`.

Notes: This is only required for App Services which require authentication. Enabling on site like a marketing or support website will prevent unauthenticated access which would be undesirable. Adding Authentication requirement will increase cost of App Service and require additional security components to facilitate the authentication

CheckTitle: App Service web app redirects HTTP to HTTPS
Description: **Azure App Service web apps** redirect `HTTP` traffic to `HTTPS` when the `HTTPS Only` setting is enabled. This evaluation identifies apps that do not force secure transport by checking whether plaintext requests are automatically redirected to encrypted endpoints.
Risk: Leaving **HTTP accessible** enables **man-in-the-middle** interception, credential and cookie theft, and response tampering. This undermines **confidentiality** and **integrity**, and can lead to session hijacking or downgrade attacks that bypass TLS.

Code.Terraform:
```hcl
# Enforce HTTPS-only on an App Service
resource "azurerm_windows_web_app" "<example_resource_name>" {
  name                = "<example_resource_name>"
  resource_group_name = "<example_resource_name>"
  location            = "<example_location>"
  service_plan_id     = "<example_resource_id>"

  https_only = true # Critical: redirects HTTP to HTTPS
}
```
Code.CLI: az webapp update --resource-group <RESOURCE_GROUP_NAME> --name <APP_NAME> --set httpsOnly=true
Code.Other:
1. Sign in to the Azure portal and go to App Services
2. Select your web app
3. Go to TLS/SSL settings and set HTTPS Only to On
4. Click Save

Recommendation.Text:
Enforce **HTTPS-only** for all apps.
- Use trusted certificates and require `TLS 1.2` or later
- Enable **HSTS** to prevent downgrade/mixed-content
- Redirect legacy `http` links to `https`
- Minimize HTTP exposure via WAF/CDN or private access
Apply **defense in depth** to protect data in transit.

Notes: When it is enabled, every incoming HTTP request is redirected to the HTTPS port. This means an extra level of security will be added to the HTTP requests made to the app.

CheckTitle: App Service web app uses the latest supported Java version or 17 by default
Description:
**Azure App Service web apps** that run **Java** are assessed to ensure their configured runtime uses the **latest supported major version** (LTS) for the environment, across Linux and Windows.

*Only apps with Java enabled are considered.*
Risk: Using an **outdated Java runtime** enables known exploits like **remote code execution**, unsafe **deserialization**, and **cryptographic flaws**, risking data theft and tampering (**confidentiality, integrity**) and outages or takeover (**availability**). Unsupported versions also delay critical security patches.

Code.CLI: az webapp config set --resource-group <RESOURCE_GROUP> --name <APP_NAME> --linux-fx-version "JAVA|17-java17"
Code.Other:
1. In the Azure portal, go to App Services and open your web app
2. Select Settings > Configuration > General settings
3. For Linux apps: under Stack settings, choose Java and set Java version to 17 (or choose Tomcat/JBoss with Java version 17)
4. For Windows apps: under Stack settings, set Java version to 17
5. Click Save and restart if prompted

Recommendation.Text:
Adopt the **latest supported LTS Java** (`java <latest LTS>`) and standardize on that major line.
- Enable automatic minor/patch updates
- Validate upgrades in a staging environment before production
- Retire deprecated runtimes and track vendor EOL

Apply **change management** and **defense in depth** to reduce exposure.

Notes: If your app is written using version-dependent features or libraries, they may not be available on the latest version. If you wish to upgrade, research the impact thoroughly. Upgrading may have unforeseen consequences that could result in downtime.

CheckTitle: App Service web app uses the latest supported PHP version or 8.2 by default
Description: **Azure App Service web apps** running **PHP** are evaluated to ensure the runtime is configured to the **latest supported** release. The finding compares the app's PHP stack (from `linuxFxVersion` or `php_version`) with the newest available version.
Risk: Using **outdated PHP** enables exploitation of known flaws, including **remote code execution**, causing secret disclosure (confidentiality), unauthorized changes (integrity), and crashes or downtime (availability). Deprecated versions lack patches, widening exposure and instability.

Code.CLI: az webapp config set --resource-group <RESOURCE_GROUP_NAME> --name <APP_NAME> --linux-fx-version "PHP|8.2"
Code.Other:
1. In Azure Portal, go to App Services and select your app
2. Navigate to Settings > Configuration > General settings
3. Under Stack settings, select PHP and set Version to 8.2
4. Click Save and confirm the restart

Recommendation.Text: Standardize on the **latest supported PHP** and avoid EoL releases. Update promptly after security advisories, validate in staging, and automate version governance across apps. Prefer supported Linux runtimes, limit optional extensions, and apply **defense in depth** and **least privilege** to reduce blast radius.

Notes: If your app is written using version-dependent features or libraries, they may not be available on the latest version. If you wish to upgrade, research the impact thoroughly. Upgrading may have unforeseen consequences that could result in downtime

CheckTitle: App Service web app uses the latest supported Python version or 3.12 by default
Description: **Azure App Service web apps** using **Python** are assessed to confirm the runtime is the **latest supported version** (e.g., `3.12`). The evaluation reads the app's stack configuration to detect Python usage and compares the configured runtime against the defined latest baseline.
Risk:
Outdated **Python runtimes** weaken security and reliability:
- Compromise confidentiality via known interpreter/SSL flaws
- Undermine integrity through RCE and package exploitation
- Reduce availability when deprecated versions lose patches and break under load

Code.CLI: az webapp config set --resource-group <RESOURCE_GROUP_NAME> --name <APP_NAME> --linux-fx-version "PYTHON|3.12"
Code.Other:
1. In the Azure portal, go to App Services and select your app
2. Go to Settings > Configuration > General settings
3. Under Stack settings, set Python version to 3.12
4. Click Save and confirm the restart

Recommendation.Text:
Adopt the **latest supported Python minor** for App Service and maintain a consistent upgrade policy. Track vendor EOL, test in staging, and roll out via CI/CD.

Apply **defense in depth**: minimize privileges and enforce strong TLS to reduce exposure during updates.

Notes: If your app is written using version-dependent features or libraries, they may not be available on the latest version. If you wish to upgrade, research the impact thoroughly. Upgrading may have unforeseen consequences that could result in downtime.

CheckTitle: App Service web app has HTTP/2.0 enabled
Description: **Azure App Service web apps** are evaluated for **HTTP/2 support** via the `http20_enabled` configuration, indicating whether the site serves traffic using the HTTP/2 protocol
Risk: Without **HTTP/2**, apps remain on **HTTP/1.1**, increasing connection overhead and head-of-line blocking, which can reduce **availability** under load. Inefficient use of TLS sessions raises **DoS susceptibility** and degrades user experience, impacting service reliability

Code.CLI: az webapp config set --resource-group <RESOURCE_GROUP_NAME> --name <APP_NAME> --http20-enabled true
Code.Other:
1. Sign in to the Azure portal and go to App Services
2. Select your web app
3. Navigate to Settings > Configuration > General settings
4. Set HTTP version to 2.0
5. Click Save

Recommendation.Text:
Enable **HTTP/2** (`http20_enabled=true`) to use a modern, efficient transport.

- Enforce `HTTPS Only` and a strong minimum `TLS` version for defense-in-depth
- Validate app/library compatibility before rollout
- Monitor performance and errors post-change; deploy gradually

Notes: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/security/benchmark/azure/security-controls-v3-posture-vulnerability-management#pv-7-rapidly-and-automatically-remediate-software-vulnerabilities

CheckTitle: App Service web app has FTP disabled or FTPS-only enforced
Description: **Azure App Service web apps** are evaluated for **FTP exposure** via the `ftpsState` setting. Values `FtpsOnly` or `Disabled` indicate FTP is not allowed; `AllAllowed` means both FTP and FTPS are accepted.
Risk:
Allowing **FTP (unencrypted)** exposes credentials on public endpoints, enabling **credential theft** and **session hijacking**.

Compromise grants write access to code and content, enabling **malicious deployments**, backdoors, and data leakage, degrading **integrity** and **confidentiality**-with greater blast radius if shared, user-scope publishing credentials are used.

Code.CLI: az webapp config set --resource-group <RESOURCE_GROUP> --name <APP_NAME> --ftps-state FtpsOnly
Code.Other:
1. In Azure Portal, go to App Services and select your app
2. Go to Settings > Configuration > General settings
3. Set FTP state to FTPS only (or Disabled)
4. Click Save

Recommendation.Text:
Disable FTP or enforce **FTPS** (`ftpsState: FtpsOnly` or `Disabled`).

Prefer **CI/CD** over manual FTP and apply **least privilege** with app-scoped credentials. Rotate publishing secrets, enforce modern TLS, and restrict access via private networking. *If FTP is unavoidable*, require FTPS and monitor publishing logs.

Notes: Any deployment workflows that rely on FTP or FTPs rather than the WebDeploy or HTTPs endpoints may be affected.

CheckTitle: Function app has function keys configured
Description:
**Azure Function apps** are evaluated for configured **function access keys** on HTTP endpoints.

The finding distinguishes functions with at least one access key defined from those without any keys configured.
Risk:
Missing **access keys** weakens authentication, enabling unsolicited calls to function endpoints. This risks:
- loss of **confidentiality** via data exposure
- compromised **integrity** by triggering unintended actions
- reduced **availability** from abuse, throttling, and cost spikes

Code.CLI: az functionapp function keys set --resource-group <RESOURCE_GROUP> --name <FUNCTION_APP_NAME> --function-name <FUNCTION_NAME> --key-name default --key-value <KEY_VALUE>
Code.Other:
1. Sign in to the Azure portal and go to your Function App
2. Select Functions, then click the specific function
3. Open Function keys (or API keys)
4. Click Add (New function key), set Name (e.g., default) and value (or generate)
5. Save to create the key

Recommendation.Text:
Enforce **function keys** for non-public endpoints and apply **least privilege**:
- avoid `anonymous` when not required
- rotate keys; don't share the `admin` key
- enable **App Service Authentication** or **API Management** for identity-aware access
- restrict inbound networks and monitor logs
- store and rotate secrets in **Key Vault**

Notes: For additional security, consider using managed identities and key vaults along with access keys. This provides granular control over resource access and improves auditability.

CheckTitle: Function App has Application Insights configured
Description: **Azure Function apps** are configured to send telemetry to **Application Insights** when application settings include `APPLICATIONINSIGHTS_CONNECTION_STRING` or `APPINSIGHTS_INSTRUMENTATIONKEY`.
Risk: Without this telemetry, **visibility** into exceptions, dependencies, and performance is lost, reducing **availability** and delaying response. Gaps in traces mask anomalous traffic and failures, enabling prolonged outages and undermining **integrity** of processing (e.g., undetected retries or timeouts).

Code.CLI: az functionapp config appsettings set --resource-group <RESOURCE_GROUP> --name <FUNCTION_APP_NAME> --settings APPLICATIONINSIGHTS_CONNECTION_STRING=<CONNECTION_STRING>
Code.Other:
1. In Azure Portal, go to Function App > Configuration > Application settings
2. Click + New application setting
3. Name: APPLICATIONINSIGHTS_CONNECTION_STRING
4. Value: paste the connection string from your Application Insights resource (Overview > Connection string)
5. Click OK, then Save
6. If prompted, click Continue to apply the changes

Recommendation.Text: Enable **Application Insights** for each Function App using a `APPLICATIONINSIGHTS_CONNECTION_STRING` and standardize telemetry. Apply **defense in depth**: use distributed tracing, alert on errors/latency, and enforce least-privilege access and retention on logs to prevent blind spots and speed recovery.

CheckTitle: Function app has FTP and FTPS deployments disabled
Description: **Azure Function apps** are evaluated for the `ftps_state` setting that controls **FTP/FTPS deployment endpoints**. Values `AllAllowed` or `FtpsOnly` indicate deployment over FTP/FTPS is enabled, while `Disabled` indicates both endpoints are turned off.
Risk: Enabled **FTP/FTPS deployment** undermines confidentiality and integrity. FTP exposes credentials in cleartext; FTPS still presents a public basic-auth endpoint susceptible to brute force and credential reuse. Compromise enables **unauthorized code pushes**, leading to RCE, data leakage, and service disruption.

Code.Terraform:
```hcl
# Disable FTP and FTPS on a Function App
resource "azurerm_linux_function_app" "<example_resource_name>" {
  name                       = "<example_resource_name>"
  resource_group_name        = "<example_resource_name>"
  location                   = "<example_location>"
  service_plan_id            = "<example_resource_id>"
  storage_account_name       = "<example_resource_name>"
  storage_account_access_key = "<example_secret_value>"
  functions_extension_version = "~4"

  site_config {
    ftps_state = "Disabled" # CRITICAL: Disables both FTP and FTPS deployments
  }
}
```
Code.CLI: az webapp config set --resource-group <resource-group> --name <app-name> --ftps-state Disabled
Code.Other:
1. In the Azure portal, go to your Function App
2. Select Configuration > General settings
3. Under Platform settings, set FTP state to Disabled
4. Click Save

Recommendation.Text: Disable **FTP and FTPS deployment** on Function apps (`ftps_state: Disabled`). Adopt **defense in depth**: deploy via **CI/CD** with packaged artifacts (zip or containers), enforce **least privilege** publishing access, and limit exposure of build and deployment endpoints. *If unavoidable, use FTPS-only with TLS 1.2 and rotate credentials promptly.*

Notes: This check ensures that Azure Functions are deployed securely, reducing the attack surface and protecting sensitive information.

CheckTitle: Function app has a system-assigned or user-assigned managed identity enabled
Description:
**Azure Function Apps** are evaluated for an enabled **managed identity** (`SystemAssigned` or `UserAssigned`) configured on the app.

The finding indicates whether an identity is present to support token-based access to other Azure resources.
Risk:
Without **managed identities**, apps rely on stored secrets/keys, risking:
- Confidentiality loss from leaked credentials
- Integrity tampering via unauthorized writes
- Availability outages from secret expiry/rotation

Compromised keys enable unauthorized access and lateral movement.

Code.CLI: az functionapp identity assign --resource-group <resource_group> --name <function_name>
Code.Other:
1. In Azure Portal, go to your Function App
2. Under Settings, select Identity
3. On the System assigned tab, set Status to On
4. Click Save

Recommendation.Text: Enable a **managed identity** on each Function App (`SystemAssigned` per app, `UserAssigned` for shared/long-lived needs). Replace secrets with token-based access and grant only required RBAC roles (**least privilege**). Remove keys from settings, apply **separation of duties**, and monitor access as part of **defense in depth**.

CheckTitle: Function app managed identity is not assigned Owner, Contributor, User Access Administrator, or Role Based Access Control Administrator roles
Description:
**Azure Function apps** with managed identities are evaluated for assignments to broad **administrative roles**: **Owner**, **Contributor**, **User Access Administrator**, **RBAC Administrator**.

The finding highlights functions whose identity carries elevated permissions beyond normal runtime needs.
Risk:
Admin rights on a function's identity expose the control plane.
- Confidentiality: read secrets and data
- Integrity: alter configs, grant roles, deploy changes
- Availability: stop or delete resources
A runtime compromise can enable **lateral movement** and **privilege escalation** across the environment.

Code.CLI: az role assignment delete --assignee <MANAGED_IDENTITY_PRINCIPAL_ID> --scope <SCOPE_ID>
Code.Other:
1. In the Azure portal, open the scope where the role is assigned (e.g., Subscription, Resource group, or the Function App resource)
2. Go to Access control (IAM) > Role assignments
3. In the Principal filter, search for the Function App's managed identity (<function-app-name>)
4. For each assignment with role Owner, Contributor, User Access Administrator, or Role Based Access Control Administrator, click Remove
5. Repeat steps 1-4 at all relevant scopes (subscription, resource group, and Function App) until no such admin roles remain for this identity

Recommendation.Text:
Apply **least privilege**: grant only narrowly scoped, data-plane permissions needed by the function; avoid broad roles like `Owner` or `Contributor`.
Use **separation of duties** and **just-in-time** elevation for rare admin tasks.
Regularly review role assignments and restrict scope to the smallest necessary boundary.

Notes: This check helps prevent privilege escalation attacks and ensures that Azure functions operate with the necessary permissions, reducing the impact of potential security breaches.

CheckTitle: Function app uses the latest supported runtime version (~4)
Description: **Azure Function apps** are assessed for the **runtime version** set via `FUNCTIONS_EXTENSION_VERSION`. The finding identifies apps not configured to use the current supported major version `~4`.
Risk:
Outdated Functions runtimes erode CIA:
- **Confidentiality**: known flaws enable unauthorized data access.
- **Integrity**: RCE or binding bugs allow code tampering.
- **Availability**: missing fixes cause crashes and scale faults.

End-of-support versions (e.g., 2.x/3.x) lack security patches, increasing exploitability.

Code.CLI: az functionapp config appsettings set --name <function_app_name> --resource-group <resource_group_name> --settings FUNCTIONS_EXTENSION_VERSION=~4
Code.Other:
1. In the Azure portal, go to Function App <example_resource_name>
2. Select Configuration > Application settings
3. Add or edit the setting:
   - Name: FUNCTIONS_EXTENSION_VERSION
   - Value: ~4
4. Click Save and confirm the restart
5. Verify the setting shows FUNCTIONS_EXTENSION_VERSION = ~4

Recommendation.Text:
Standardize on supported runtime `~4` and align language/extension versions.
- Enforce upgrades in CI/CD and use staging to validate before rollout.
- Apply **least privilege** for app identities and secrets.
- Prefer automated patching and periodic reviews to avoid drift; avoid downgrades or indefinite minor pinning.

Notes: Stay informed about the latest security updates and patch releases for Azure Functions to maintain a secure and up-to-date environment.

CheckTitle: Function app is not publicly accessible
Description: **Azure Function apps** are assessed for whether they are reachable from the public Internet. The evaluation considers the app's `publicNetworkAccess` state and the presence of access restrictions or private endpoints to limit inbound traffic.
Risk: Public exposure allows unauthorized invocation, risking data disclosure and tampering (**confidentiality** and **integrity**). Attackers can brute-force tokens or abuse misconfigurations for remote execution. Unrestricted calls also enable abuse and DoS, driving cost and harming **availability**.

Code.Terraform:
```hcl
# Disable public network access for the Function App
resource "azurerm_linux_function_app" "<example_resource_name>" {
  name                       = "<example_resource_name>"
  location                   = azurerm_resource_group.main.location
  resource_group_name        = azurerm_resource_group.main.name
  service_plan_id            = azurerm_service_plan.main.id
  storage_account_name       = azurerm_storage_account.main.name
  storage_account_access_key = azurerm_storage_account.main.primary_access_key

  public_network_access_enabled = false # Critical: disables public endpoint access
}
```
Code.CLI: az functionapp update --resource-group <RESOURCE_GROUP> --name <FUNCTION_APP_NAME> --set publicNetworkAccess=Disabled
Code.Other:
1. In the Azure portal, go to your Function App
2. Select Networking
3. Under Public access, set Public network access to Disabled
4. Click Save

Recommendation.Text:
Apply network isolation and least privilege:
- Set `publicNetworkAccess=Disabled`
- Use access restrictions for trusted IPs/VNets or **Private Endpoints**
- Require strong auth (e.g., **Microsoft Entra ID**) over shared keys
- Front with **API Management/WAF**
- Keep secrets in **Key Vault** and monitor access logs

CheckTitle: Function app has Virtual Network integration enabled
Description:
**Azure Function apps** configured with **Virtual Network integration** uses a chosen subnet so outbound traffic is routed via the VNet and can reach private or service-endpoint-secured resources.

The finding reflects whether a function app is associated with a subnet resource ID.
Risk:
Without VNet integration, function apps send egress directly to the public Internet and cannot reach private endpoints.

This weakens confidentiality and integrity by bypassing NSG/UDR controls, enables data exfiltration from compromised code, and may force exposing backends publicly, increasing attack surface.

Code.Terraform:
```hcl
# Enable VNet integration for an existing Function App
resource "azurerm_app_service_virtual_network_swift_connection" "<example_resource_name>" {
  app_service_id = "/subscriptions/<example_resource_id>/resourceGroups/<example_resource_name>/providers/Microsoft.Web/sites/<example_resource_name>" # CRITICAL: target Function App resource ID
  subnet_id      = "/subscriptions/<example_resource_id>/resourceGroups/<example_resource_name>/providers/Microsoft.Network/virtualNetworks/<example_resource_name>/subnets/<example_resource_name>" # CRITICAL: subnet to integrate with
}
```
Code.CLI: az functionapp vnet-integration add --name <function_app_name> --resource-group <resource_group_name> --vnet <vnet_name> --subnet <subnet_name>
Code.Other:
1. In the Azure portal, go to your Function App
2. Select Networking > VNet Integration
3. Click Add VNet
4. Choose the target Virtual network and Subnet
5. Click OK/Save to apply

Recommendation.Text:
Enable **Virtual Network integration** and attach function apps to a dedicated subnet to enforce **least privilege network access**.

Route egress through the VNet (e.g., `Route All`), apply **NSGs/UDRs**, and use **private endpoints** or service endpoints for dependencies. Restrict outbound traffic by default as part of **defense in depth**.

CheckTitle: App Service web app has HTTP logs enabled in diagnostic settings
Description: **Azure App Service web apps** diagnostic settings include **HTTP request logging** when the `AppServiceHTTPLogs` category (or the `allLogs` group) is enabled to capture web access events.
Risk: Without **HTTP access logs**, visibility into requests is lost, hindering **detection** of brute force, probing, and injection attempts. This weakens **forensics** and reduces **confidentiality** and **integrity** by masking data access paths and blocking reliable incident timelines.

Code.Terraform:
```hcl
# Enable HTTP Logs for App Service via Azure Monitor diagnostic setting
resource "azurerm_monitor_diagnostic_setting" "<example_resource_name>" {
  name                       = "<example_resource_name>"
  target_resource_id         = "/subscriptions/<SUBSCRIPTION_ID>/resourceGroups/<RESOURCE_GROUP>/providers/Microsoft.Web/sites/<example_resource_name>"
  log_analytics_workspace_id = "<example_resource_id>" # Destination Log Analytics workspace

  log {                      # Critical: enables the HTTP Logs category
    category = "AppServiceHTTPLogs"
    enabled  = true
  }
}
```
Code.CLI: az monitor diagnostic-settings create --name <example_resource_name> --resource /subscriptions/<SUBSCRIPTION_ID>/resourceGroups/<RESOURCE_GROUP>/providers/Microsoft.Web/sites/<APP_NAME> --workspace <LOG_ANALYTICS_WORKSPACE_RESOURCE_ID> --logs '[{"category":"AppServiceHTTPLogs","enabled":true}]'
Code.Other:
1. In Azure Portal, go to your App Service > Monitoring > Diagnostic settings
2. Click + Add diagnostic setting
3. Under Logs, check AppServiceHTTPLogs (or select the allLogs category group)
4. Choose a destination (Log Analytics workspace, Storage account, or Event Hub)
5. Click Save

Recommendation.Text: Enable **diagnostic settings** with `AppServiceHTTPLogs` (or `allLogs`) and route logs to a centralized store. Enforce **least privilege**, retention, and tamper-resistant storage. Integrate with a **SIEM** for analytics and alerting, and periodically verify logging coverage across all apps and regions.

Notes: Log consumption and processing will incur additional cost.

CheckTitle: App Service web app has minimum TLS version set to 1.2 or 1.3
Description: **Azure App Service web apps** are assessed for the configured minimum TLS version for HTTPS. The expected baseline is `1.2` or `1.3`; settings that permit lower versions indicate acceptance of legacy TLS during client negotiation.
Risk: Allowing `TLS 1.0/1.1` enables protocol downgrades and weak cipher negotiation, exposing HTTPS traffic to **MITM** interception, credential theft, and tampering. This undermines the **confidentiality** and **integrity** of sessions and data in transit, and can enable account takeover via stolen tokens.

Code.CLI: az webapp config set --resource-group <RESOURCE_GROUP_NAME> --name <APP_NAME> --min-tls-version 1.2
Code.Other:
1. Sign in to Azure Portal and go to App Services
2. Select your app
3. Go to Settings > Configuration > General settings
4. Set Minimum TLS Version to 1.2 (or 1.3 if available)
5. Click Save

Recommendation.Text: Enforce a minimum of `TLS 1.2` (prefer `1.3`) and disable `1.0/1.1`. Require **HTTPS-only**, enable HSTS, and align with modern cipher suites. Test client compatibility and phase out legacy agents. Document narrow exceptions with compensating controls to uphold **defense in depth** and prevent downgrades.

Notes: By default, TLS Version feature will be set to 1.2 when a new app is created using the command-line tool or Azure Portal console.

CheckTitle: App Service web app has a managed identity configured
Description: **Azure App Service web apps** are configured with a **managed identity** (`identity`: `SystemAssigned` or `UserAssigned`) for token-based access to Azure resources without embedded credentials
Risk: **Missing managed identity** drives reliance on stored secrets. Leaked credentials enable **unauthorized access** to SQL, Storage, or Key Vault, leading to **data exfiltration**, tampering, and lateral movement. Secret expiry or revocation can break connectivity, degrading **availability**.

Code.CLI: az webapp identity assign --resource-group <RESOURCE_GROUP_NAME> --name <APP_NAME>
Code.Other:
1. Sign in to the Azure portal
2. Go to App Services and select your app
3. Under Settings, select Identity
4. On the System assigned tab, set Status to On
5. Click Save and confirm

Recommendation.Text: Enable a **managed identity** and use it for all service-to-service access. Apply **least privilege** on target resources and eliminate secrets from code and app settings. Remove legacy credentials, rotate residual keys, and monitor usage for **defense in depth**. *Use system-assigned per app; user-assigned for reuse or separation.*

Notes: By default, Managed service identity via Azure AD is disabled.

CheckTitle: Subscription has at least one Application Insights resource configured
Description:
**Azure subscription** contains at least one **Application Insights** resource collecting application telemetry (metrics, traces, logs) for monitored workloads.

The check determines whether telemetry collection exists at the subscription level, indicating that application monitoring is configured.
Risk:
If **Application Insights** is missing, applications run with reduced **observability**, limiting detection of anomalies and attacks.

This undermines **integrity** and accountability (fewer traces), degrades **availability** by slowing troubleshooting, and increases exposure to undetected data exfiltration or injection at the app layer.

Code.Terraform:
```hcl
# Critical: This resource creates an Application Insights component to satisfy the check
resource "azurerm_application_insights" "main" {
  name                = "<example_resource_name>"
  location            = "<location>"
  resource_group_name = "<example_resource_name>"
  application_type    = "web" # Critical: ensures creation of the component
}
```
Code.CLI: az monitor app-insights component create --app <APP_NAME> --resource-group <RESOURCE_GROUP> --location <LOCATION> --application-type web --subscription <SUBSCRIPTION_ID>
Code.Other:
1. In the Azure portal, go to Azure Monitor > Application Insights
2. Click Create
3. Select a Subscription and Resource group
4. Enter a Name and choose a Region
5. Click Review + create, then Create
6. Verify the resource appears under Application Insights in the selected subscription

Recommendation.Text: Deploy **Application Insights** for all critical workloads and centralize data in a **Log Analytics workspace**. Configure actionable alerts and dashboards, enforce **least privilege** on telemetry, and set retention/export policies. Use private connectivity and appropriate sampling, and integrate with SIEM for **defense in depth**.

Notes: Because Application Insights relies on a Log Analytics Workspace, an organization will incur additional expenses when using this service.

CheckTitle: Container Registry admin user is disabled
Description: **Azure Container Registry** admin account configuration, confirming the built-in **admin user** is disabled so access relies on Microsoft Entra-based **RBAC** identities and scoped roles.
Risk: Using a shared, always-valid **admin credential** grants full push/pull and lacks attribution. Compromise enables unauthorized image pulls (confidentiality), malicious pushes or tag changes (integrity), and deletions or lockout (availability), enabling supply-chain attacks and lateral movement.

Code.Terraform:
```hcl
resource "azurerm_container_registry" "example" {
  name                = "<example_resource_name>"
  resource_group_name = "<example_resource_name>"
  location            = "<location>"
  sku                 = "<SKU_NAME>"

  admin_enabled = false # Critical: disables ACR admin user to pass the check
}
```
Code.CLI: az acr update --name <RegistryName> --resource-group <ResourceGroupName> --admin-enabled false
Code.Other:
1. In Azure Portal, go to Container registries and select your registry
2. Under Settings, open Access keys
3. Set Admin user to Disabled
4. Click Save

Recommendation.Text: Disable the **admin account** and require Microsoft Entra-backed **RBAC**. Assign least-privilege roles to users, service principals, or managed identities. Prefer short-lived credentials, rotate any residual secrets, and apply defense-in-depth with network restrictions and continuous auditing of registry access.

Notes: The transition away from using the admin user to RBAC will facilitate a more secure and manageable access model, minimizing the potential risk of unauthorized access to your container images.

CheckTitle: Container Registry public network access is disabled
Description: **Azure Container Registry** configuration indicates whether the registry permits **unrestricted public access** based on the `Public network access` setting.
Risk:
**Internet-exposed ACR** expands attack paths impacting **CIA**:
- Confidentiality: unauthorized image pulls leak code/secrets
- Integrity: compromised creds allow tampered image pushes (supply-chain)
- Availability: pull storms or scans exhaust quotas, causing outages and cost spikes

Code.Terraform:
```hcl
resource "azurerm_container_registry" "<example_resource_name>" {
  name                = "<example_resource_name>"
  resource_group_name = "<example_resource_name>"
  location            = "<location>"
  sku                 = "Basic"

  public_network_access_enabled = false # Critical: disables public endpoint to block unrestricted access
}
```
Code.CLI: az acr update --name <registry-name> --public-network-enabled false
Code.Other:
1. In the Azure portal, go to your Container Registry
2. Select Settings > Networking
3. On Public access, set Allow public network access to Disabled
4. Click Save

Recommendation.Text:
Set `Public network access` to `Disabled` and use **Private Link** for registry access.

If public reachability is required, allow only **selected IPs**, enforce **least privilege** and token rotation, and apply **defense in depth** (egress control, network segmentation, logging of push/pull events).

Notes: This feature is only available for Premium SKU registries.

CheckTitle: Container Registry uses a private endpoint (Private Link)
Description: **Azure Container Registry** access via **Private Endpoints** (Azure Private Link). Registries with `private endpoint connections` use private IPs; others rely on the public endpoint.
Risk: Publicly reachable registries expand attack surface for **credential stuffing**, token abuse, and scanning. A compromise enables unauthorized pull/push, causing image **data leakage** and **supply-chain tampering**. Public routing weakens network isolation, impacting the **confidentiality** and **integrity** of images and metadata.

Code.CLI: az network private-endpoint create --resource-group <example_resource_name> --name <example_resource_name> --vnet-name <example_resource_name> --subnet <example_resource_name> --private-connection-resource-id <example_resource_id> --group-ids registry --connection-name <example_resource_name>
Code.Other:
1. In Azure Portal, go to Container registries > select your registry
2. Navigate to Settings > Networking > Private endpoints tab
3. Click + Private endpoint, enter a name, select your VNet and Subnet
4. Set Resource type to Microsoft.ContainerRegistry/registries and Target subresource to registry
5. Click Review + create, then Create

Recommendation.Text:
Use **Private Link** with **private endpoints** and set `Public network access: Disabled`.
- Restrict access to trusted VNets/subnets
- Prefer private endpoints over service endpoints
- Enforce **least privilege** on registry actions
- Configure private DNS for the registry FQDN
- Monitor access logs for **defense in depth**

Notes: This feature is only available for Premium SKU registries.

CheckTitle: Cosmos DB account firewall allows access only from selected networks
Description:
**Azure Cosmos DB accounts** limit connectivity to **selected networks** using virtual network rules and/or IP allowlists rather than permitting access from all networks.

The evaluation determines whether the account's network firewall enforces this restriction.
Risk:
Access from all networks enlarges the attack surface. If keys or tokens are exposed or privileges are misconfigured, attackers anywhere can read or modify data, harming **confidentiality** and **integrity**.

Weak segmentation also enables SSRF/pivot paths from Azure services and can impact **availability** through abuse.

Code.CLI: az cosmosdb network-rule add -g <RESOURCE_GROUP> -n <ACCOUNT_NAME> --subnet <example_resource_id>
Code.Other:
1. In Azure Portal, open your Cosmos DB account
2. Go to Settings > Networking
3. Select Selected networks
4. Click Add existing virtual network, choose the VNet and Subnet, then click Enable and Add
5. Click Save

Recommendation.Text:
Set network access to `Selected networks` with **least privilege**:
- Prefer **private endpoints** or VNet service endpoints with subnet ACLs
- Keep IP allowlists minimal; avoid `0.0.0.0`
- *When feasible*, set `publicNetworkAccess=Disabled` with Private Link
- Apply **defense in depth** and monitor access and firewall changes

Notes: Failure to whitelist the correct networks will result in a connection loss.

CheckTitle: Cosmos DB account has local authentication disabled and uses Azure AD authentication with Azure RBAC
Description: **Azure Cosmos DB accounts** configured to use **Microsoft Entra ID** with **Azure RBAC** by disabling key-based credentials (`disableLocalAuth=true`). Clients authenticate with identities rather than account keys.
Risk: With local/key-based auth enabled, **long-lived account keys** can be leaked or shared, enabling unauthorized reads/writes and tampering. Access bypasses **MFA** and granular **RBAC**, hindering rotation/revocation and increasing persistence and lateral movement risks.

Code.Terraform:
```hcl
# Terraform: Disable local (key-based) auth on a Cosmos DB account
resource "azurerm_cosmosdb_account" "<example_resource_name>" {
  name                = "<example_resource_name>"
  resource_group_name = "<example_resource_name>"
  location            = "<example_resource_name>"
  offer_type          = "Standard"
  kind                = "GlobalDocumentDB"

  geo_location {
    location          = "<example_resource_name>"
    failover_priority = 0
  }

  local_authentication_disabled = true # Critical: Disables key-based auth to enforce Entra ID + RBAC
}
```
Code.CLI: az resource update --resource-group <RESOURCE_GROUP> --name <COSMOS_ACCOUNT_NAME> --resource-type Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts --set properties.disableLocalAuth=true
Code.Other:
1. Sign in to the Azure portal and open your Cosmos DB account
2. In the left menu, select Keys
3. Turn on Disable key-based authentication (Disable local authentication)
4. Click Save

Recommendation.Text: Disable local authentication by setting `disableLocalAuth=true` and require **Entra ID + Azure RBAC** for control and data access. Use **managed identities**, apply **least privilege** roles, retire shared keys, and enforce **zero trust** with conditional access and short-lived credentials.

CheckTitle: Cosmos DB account uses private endpoint connections
Description: **Azure Cosmos DB accounts** are assessed for **private endpoint connections** that keep data-plane traffic on private IPs within authorized virtual networks.
Risk:
Without **private endpoints**, access may use public endpoints or broad IP rules, enabling:
- interception and credential replay
- unauthorized queries and data exfiltration
- lateral movement via exposed paths

This degrades **confidentiality** and can impact **availability** under abusive traffic.

Code.Terraform:
```hcl
# Create a Private Endpoint to a Cosmos DB account (adds a private endpoint connection)
resource "azurerm_private_endpoint" "<example_resource_name>" {
  name                = "<example_resource_name>"
  location            = "<location>"
  resource_group_name = "<example_resource_name>"
  subnet_id           = "<example_subnet_id>"

  private_service_connection {
    name                           = "<example_resource_name>"
    private_connection_resource_id = "<example_cosmosdb_account_id>" # CRITICAL: Cosmos DB account ID
    subresource_names              = ["Sql"]                           # CRITICAL: targets Cosmos DB subresource to create the connection
  }
}
```
Code.CLI: az network private-endpoint create --name <example_resource_name> --resource-group <example_resource_name> --vnet-name <example_resource_name> --subnet <example_resource_name> --private-connection-resource-id /subscriptions/<SUBSCRIPTION_ID>/resourceGroups/<example_resource_name>/providers/Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts/<example_resource_name> --group-ids Sql --connection-name <example_resource_name>
Code.Other:
1. In Azure Portal, open your Cosmos DB account
2. Go to Networking > Private access
3. Click + Private endpoint
4. Resource type: Microsoft.AzureCosmosDB/databaseAccounts; Resource: select your account; Target subresource: Sql
5. Select your Virtual network and Subnet
6. Click Review + create, then Create
7. Verify the private endpoint connection appears under Networking > Private access

Recommendation.Text:
Adopt **Azure Private Link** for Cosmos DB:
- Create private endpoints for required subresources
- Link a private DNS zone so clients resolve to private IPs
- Set `PublicNetworkAccess=Disabled`; keep tight firewall rules
- Allow only needed VNets/subnets; apply NSGs
- Enforce least privilege and monitor access patterns

Notes: Only whitelisted services will have access to communicate with the Cosmos DB.

CheckTitle: Databricks workspace uses a customer-managed key (CMK) for encryption at rest
Description: **Azure Databricks workspaces** are evaluated for use of **customer-managed keys** (`CMK`) on at-rest encryption, based on the workspace's managed disk encryption configuration.
Risk:
Without **CMK**, keys are provider-controlled, degrading **confidentiality** and incident response.
- Slower revoke/rotate during breaches
- Weaker **separation of duties** and audit trails
- Larger blast radius if storage or control plane is compromised

Code.Terraform:
```hcl
resource "azurerm_databricks_workspace" "<example_resource_name>" {
  name                = "<example_resource_name>"
  resource_group_name = "<example_resource_name>"
  location            = "<region>"
  sku                 = "premium"

  customer_managed_key_enabled      = true  # CRITICAL: enable CMK
  managed_disk_cmk_key_vault_key_id = "<example_resource_id>" # CRITICAL: key ID (Key Vault key) for managed disks
}
```
Code.CLI: az databricks workspace update --name <workspace_name> --resource-group <resource_group_name> --key-source Microsoft.Keyvault --key-name <key_name> --key-vault https://<key_vault_name>.vault.azure.net/ --key-version <key_version>
Code.Other:
1. In Azure Portal, go to your Databricks workspace
2. Select Settings > Encryption (or Customer-managed keys)
3. If prompted, click Prepare encryption and wait for completion
4. Set Key source to Microsoft Key Vault
5. Select the Key Vault key and specific key version for managed disks
6. Save to apply customer-managed key encryption

Recommendation.Text:
Enable `CMK` for workspace encryption via **Key Vault** or **Managed HSM** and enforce:
- Least privilege for key usage
- Regular rotation and retire old versions
- Audit logging and alerts on key ops
- Separation of duties for key vs data roles
- Deny-by-default policies limiting scope

Notes: Customer-managed key (CMK) encryption is only available for Databricks workspaces on the Premium tier.

CheckTitle: Databricks workspace is deployed in a customer-managed VNet (VNet Injection enabled)
Description: **Azure Databricks workspaces** using **VNet injection** are placed in a customer-managed VNet rather than a Databricks-managed network. This evaluates whether a workspace is linked to a customer VNet.
Risk:
Using a Databricks-managed VNet limits control over routing, egress, and access boundaries, degrading **confidentiality** and **integrity**.
- Unrestricted outbound paths enable **data exfiltration**
- Harder to enforce **private endpoints** and NSG policies
- Increased chance of **lateral movement** into compute nodes

Code.Terraform:
```hcl
# Azure Databricks workspace with VNet injection
resource "azurerm_databricks_workspace" "<example_resource_name>" {
  name                = "<example_resource_name>"
  resource_group_name = "<example_resource_name>"
  location            = "<region>"
  sku                 = "premium"

  custom_parameters {
    virtual_network_id  = "/subscriptions/<example_resource_id>/resourceGroups/<example_resource_name>/providers/Microsoft.Network/virtualNetworks/<example_resource_name>" # CRITICAL: Enables VNet injection by using your VNet
    public_subnet_name  = "<example_resource_name>-public"   # Required: host (public) subnet
    private_subnet_name = "<example_resource_name>-private"  # Required: container (private) subnet
  }
}
```
Code.CLI: az databricks workspace create --name <workspace_name> --resource-group <resource_group_name> --location <region> --sku premium --vnet /subscriptions/<subscription_id>/resourceGroups/<resource_group_name>/providers/Microsoft.Network/virtualNetworks/<vnet_name> --public-subnet <public_subnet_name> --private-subnet <private_subnet_name>
Code.Other:
1. In the Azure Portal, go to Create a resource > Azure Databricks
2. On Basics, enter workspace name, region, and resource group
3. Open the Networking tab and select Your VNet (VNet injection)
4. Choose your Virtual network and select the Host (public) and Container (private) subnets
5. Click Review + create, then Create
6. Migrate workloads to this workspace and delete the non-VNet workspace if no longer needed

Recommendation.Text:
Deploy workspaces in a customer-managed VNet and apply **defense in depth**:
- Enforce egress control with firewalls/NAT and UDRs
- Prefer **private endpoints** to public access
- Apply **least privilege** NSG rules and segregate subnets
- Use DNS controls and monitoring to detect anomalies

CheckTitle: Security contact has additional email addresses configured
Description: **Microsoft Defender for Cloud** security contact settings include **additional email recipients** defined in the `emails` field to receive alert notifications.
Risk: Relying only on subscription owners for alerts creates a **single point of failure**. Missed or delayed notifications extend attacker dwell time, enabling data exfiltration (**confidentiality**), unauthorized changes (**integrity**), and service disruption (**availability**). Absence or turnover can silently suppress alerts.

Code.CLI: az rest --method put --url https://management.azure.com/subscriptions/<SUBSCRIPTION_ID>/providers/Microsoft.Security/securityContacts/default?api-version=2020-01-01-preview --body '{ "properties": { "emails": "<EMAIL>" } }'
Code.Other:
1. Sign in to the Azure portal
2. Go to Microsoft Defender for Cloud > Environment settings
3. Select the target subscription
4. Click Email notifications
5. In Email addresses, enter at least one email (comma-separated for multiple)
6. Click Save

Recommendation.Text: Use a monitored, team-managed distribution list as the **security contact** in `emails`. Include SOC/on-call for 24/7 coverage and enable role-based notifications for redundancy. Tune severities to reduce noise while capturing high-risk events, and integrate alerts with ticketing/SIEM for **defense in depth** and rapid response.

CheckTitle: All virtual machines in the subscription have endpoint protection installed
Description: **Azure virtual machines** are assessed for the presence of an **endpoint protection (antimalware)** solution and its reported health across the subscription
Risk:
Absent or unhealthy **endpoint protection** lets malware execute on VMs, risking:
- Data exfiltration (confidentiality)
- Tampering and credential theft (integrity)
- Ransomware, cryptomining, and outages (availability)

It also enables persistence and lateral movement to other cloud resources.

Code.Terraform:
```hcl
# Install Microsoft Antimalware (endpoint protection) on a VM
resource "azurerm_virtual_machine_extension" "<example_resource_name>" {
  name                 = "IaaSAntimalware"
  virtual_machine_id   = "<example_resource_id>"
  publisher            = "Microsoft.Azure.Security"  # Critical: Antimalware extension publisher
  type                 = "IaaSAntimalware"           # Critical: installs endpoint protection
  type_handler_version = "1.5"
}
```
Code.Other:
1. In Azure Portal, go to Microsoft Defender for Cloud
2. Open Recommendations and search for "Install endpoint protection solution on virtual machines"
3. Select the recommendation, click Fix
4. Select all affected VMs and click Remediate (or Apply)
5. Wait for remediation to complete and the recommendation status to turn Healthy

Recommendation.Text: Enforce an **endpoint protection/EDR** baseline on every VM. Enable real-time protection, automatic updates, and alerting; use tamper protection and keep exclusions minimal. Apply **least privilege**, keep OS and agents patched, and continuously monitor coverage and health via Defender for Cloud.

Notes: Endpoint protection will incur an additional cost to you.

CheckTitle: Security contact has attack path email notifications enabled at or above the configured minimum risk level
Description: **Microsoft Defender for Cloud** attack path email notifications are configured per subscription with a defined **minimal risk level**, and the setting is present and meets the required threshold.
Risk: Without alerts on **exploitable attack paths**, security teams lose visibility, enabling **lateral movement**, **privilege escalation**, and **data exfiltration** before containment, degrading confidentiality, integrity, and availability.

Code.CLI: az rest --method put --uri https://management.azure.com/subscriptions/<SUBSCRIPTION_ID>/providers/Microsoft.Security/securityContacts/default?api-version=2020-01-01-preview --body '{"properties":{"emails":"admin@example.com","attackPathNotifications":{"state":"On","minimalRiskLevel":"Low"}}}'
Code.Other:
1. In Azure Portal, go to Microsoft Defender for Cloud > Environment settings
2. Select the target subscription
3. Open Email notifications
4. Enable "Notify about attack paths with the following risk level (or higher)"
5. Set Risk level to Low (or your configured minimum)
6. Click Save
